source.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out validation loss and train-validation behavior across batch sizes and repeated-data training recipes, using language-model pretraining rather than the claim's natural-label classification settings.
record.gate_note: The study tests batch size and repetition-aware recipe effects on held-out validation performance. It does not test random-label memorization, dropout, optimizer comparisons, sharpness measures, or example removal. Cited findings and the illustrative 70B extrapolation are not recorded as experimental result rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 in repeated-data language-model pretraining. Figure 3 and Table 9 compare batch sizes at matched epochs and show worse validation loss for B=512 than B=64. Most headline comparisons instead optimize stopping epochs independently; deadline comparisons do not test the fixed-epoch claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. In repeated-data pretraining, batch size produces an interior validation-loss optimum; excessively large batches generalize worse, while batches below the optimum also perform worse. Repacking and embedding regularization improve the attainable frontier and extend beneficial repetition. Short deadlines favor larger batches, while longer deadlines can favor smaller batches using fewer GPUs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains decoder-only language models on repeated natural-text data with AdamW and WSD, jointly tuning batch size, learning rate, weight decay, and epoch count; it measures validation cross-entropy rather than classification test error. Code and exact commands will be released upon acceptance.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, epoch count, unique-data-pool size, data presentation across epochs, embedding tying and decay, deadline, and GPU count change the reported outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: Repacking and embedding regularization improve validation loss at a fixed batch size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-data pretraining benefits from varying packed contexts across epochs and regularizing embeddings.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches win under short deadlines, while smaller batches using fewer GPUs can win under longer deadlines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The batch size minimizing validation loss under a time constraint depends on the deadline and resource configuration.

record.code_released: Code and exact commands will be released upon acceptance.
record.problems: Evidence is limited to dense decoder-only Transformers of 153M–1.5B parameters, DCLM-Baseline data, AdamW with WSD, and measured data pools of 0.333B–3B tokens. The study reports validation cross-entropy rather than test error, and its 70B/10T resource estimates are explicitly illustrative extrapolations.
record.rows_left_out: No other batch-sweep rows were needed to cover the reported primary batch comparisons. Downstream task results in Figure 11 are mostly figure-based and the text gives qualitative aggregate descriptions; they are not separate rows because the primary validation-loss results directly cover V5. DiLoCo comparisons concern a distinct local-optimization method and are not reported as evidence about the claim's batch-size effect.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label generalization, and comparison with natural-label training.
Width scaling beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.
Image classifiers; isolated tests of learning-rate scaling, warmup, and normalization as remedies; whether these findings extend beyond the tested dense Transformers, AdamW/WSD, and data pools.
Dropout and its interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Explicit matched-epoch batch comparisons: at E8, B=512 versus B=64 gives CE 3.124 versus 3.029; at E12, 3.198 versus 2.996. These directly establish the fixed-epoch part of V5.

Paired cross-batch mitigation results: the B=512 minus B=64 gap is 0.147 CE with SHUFFLE, 0.093 with REPACK, and 0.084 with REPACK plus tying and embedding decay. Selected epochs differ, so these establish attenuation on the optimized frontier.

The repetition-aware recipe moves the optimal batch from 64 to 128 for both smaller models. For 474M, tuned CE is 3.064 at B=64, 3.060 at B=128, and 3.105 at B=512; for 153M, it is 3.293, 3.285, and 3.322 respectively.

Robustness across three independently sampled training pools: B=64 remains optimal among B=32,64,128,256, with across-pool CE standard deviations of 0.00021–0.00318. These are data-pool replications, not clearly independent initialization-seed replications.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. The small-batch reversal in R5 is compatible with V5's workload-dependent threshold. Deadline-dependent winners do not warrant limits_scope or challenges verdicts on a fixed-epoch claim. The proposed stochastic-regularization mechanism is an interpretation, not directly isolated experimentally.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and comparison with natural-label generalization.
Widening past the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance.
Image-classification and language-model comparisons under a fixed epoch budget; the study instead optimizes epoch count and compares deadlines and batch sizes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.

rows.subject: 1.5B
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and validation losses across batch sizes over epochs.
rows.baseline: B = 64: training loss higher than B = 512 later; validation loss lower than B = 512
rows.value: B = 512: training loss drops below B = 64, while validation loss remains worse and eventually increases
rows.note: The stated pattern is described as consistent with weaker stochastic regularization at large batch sizes.
rows.check: The qualitative result is correct. Clarify that Figure 3 shows validation-selected endpoints with LR/WD selected separately for each epoch, rather than one continuous run with a fixed recipe.

rows.subject: 1.5B
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and validation losses across batch sizes over epochs.
rows.baseline: B = 64 validation loss reaches 2.977 at E20
rows.value: B = 16 eventually has lower training loss but higher validation loss than B = 64
rows.note: The authors say additional optimizer steps below B = 64 continue reducing training loss without improving held-out performance.
rows.check: B=64 has better validation loss than the smaller B=16, so the batch-effect direction is reversed, not partial. This comparison is below the observed optimum and does not challenge V5's qualification that penalties arise beyond a workload-dependent size.

rows.subject: 1.5B
rows.operation_detail: Applied positive embedding weight decay to the REPACK recipe with tied embeddings.

conditions.value: Tied embeddings and positive embedding decay versus REPACK untied embeddings, no embedding decay

reader_labels.condition: Batch-size sweep on the 153M, 474M, and 1.5B models with a 1B-token pool
reader_labels.reason: B = 64 has lower best validation CE than B = 512 for all three model sizes (R1–R3). The loss sweep is described as U-shaped, and batch size changes the train-validation relationship (R4–R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fixed 8K versus 32K optimizer-step deadlines for the 1.5B model
reader_labels.reason: The preferred batch depends on deadline: a larger batch wins at the short deadline, while a small batch on 16 GPUs wins at the longer deadline (R10–R11). Repacking and embedding decay also improve validation performance, with the study tuning epoch counts rather than fixing them (R6–R9).
